title: The Last Night
subtitle: Sunday 18 to Monday 19 September 1977: The Icehouse, Two Faces at the Door, and the Bridge at Dawn

setting.name: Camp Pinecrest, the Icehouse, the Director's House, the dock and the Outlet bridge, Sunday night 18 to Monday morning 19 September 1977
setting.description: The last night before the water goes down. At dusk on Sunday Santi Rivera (or whoever Coach has chosen) is missing, locked in the windowless Icehouse with a dead man under a tarp, and Old Glass is out of the lake in his face, and has until dawn to wear it unnamed. The Outlet is dropping: by five on Monday morning the bridge will be clear, and at 6:15 Coach means to put his spare rotor in the Suburban and drive the thing over it, and the man in the mask means to stop anything that tries. The party knows the rules now, and the name. This scenario is the night, the siege, the rescue and the bridge, and it ends at sunrise one way or another.
setting.atmosphere: Cold, clear and terribly still after two days of rain. Stars. A half moon. The lake a perfect black mirror from shore to shore, so that every lit window on the Neck is doubled in it and every face at every window is seen. Mist on the water toward morning. Sound carries for a mile: a door, a voice, the spillway. This is the night the horror stops hiding. Two of a friend at once. Two Coaches. A dead man under a tarp in the dark. And at the end, if the players have earned it, a name said aloud on the dock, and a drowned man remembering who he was.

keyLocations.name: The Icehouse
keyLocations.description: Three storeys of stone and timber by the dam, built in 1881 to hold twenty thousand tons of ice in sawdust, with walls two feet thick and no windows at all. One iron-bound door on the ground floor, padlocked from outside with the camp padlock; Coach has the key. Inside: total darkness, the smell of ninety years of wet sawdust, Pinecrest's canoes racked in winter rows, the Onan generator on its pad by the door, and, on two sawhorses under a tarp, Gene Marcotte.
features: The door: oak, iron-strapped, with an iron sill plate worn bright; a new padlock on the hasp
Total darkness inside; the generator's pull cord by the door; a lantern on a nail with no kerosene in it
The upper floors: ladders, a loading gallery, and a hatch in the roof that opens onto the slates
Gene, under the tarp, on two sawhorses
encounters: Santi Rivera, in the dark since 7:45, with Gene
Coach, who comes back at midnight and sits outside the door on an upturned canoe with the office revolver across his knees
secrets: The Icehouse is the safest place on the Neck from Old Glass: no windows, an iron sill. That is exactly why Coach chose it. Santi cannot see the thing that is wearing his face, so he cannot look it in the eyes and name himself (Rule Four), and it cannot reach him. If he stays in until dawn, and the thing is carried over the bridge, the trade is made.

Breaking in: the padlock (Mechanics DC 13 with tools, or Victor's crowbar and Heavy Work, Athletics DC 12, loud), or the roof hatch from the slates (Athletics DC 14, a long fall on a failure, 2d6). Coach, if he is guarding it, will not shoot anyone but Alvin. He will stand in the doorway with his arms out and say, 'Please, friends.'

Santi in the dark: he has been sitting with his back against Gene's sawhorse for hours because, he says, 'he shouldn't be by himself.' His Dread is 4 when found. He knows exactly what Coach did and why. He wants to see it.

keyLocations.name: The Lodge on the Last Night
keyLocations.description: Everyone else on the Neck in the lounge: Opal, Winnie, Marvin, Bev, Roscoe, whoever of the party is not out. The fire. The iron sills. The black windows, which tonight look out on a lake so still that it shows every lit pane twice.
features: Every lakeside window: a black mirror from inside, and a lit square in the lake from outside
The front and back doors' iron sills
Marvin at the piano, with the 1958 Lantern Lake Waltz on the stand
encounters: 'Santi' at the door at about 9 p.m.
Two Coaches, after midnight, if Old Glass has seen Coach's face
secrets: If anyone opens the curtains tonight, everyone in the lounge is seen by the lake (Rule One). If that includes Coach, Old Glass sees its own face, and from then on it wants nothing else. Coach knows it, and will not come into the lounge unless he is brought.

keyLocations.name: The Director's House at Night
keyLocations.description: The log house on the point, dark, its lakeside windows painted out from inside. Tonight it is the one house on the Neck the lake cannot see into, unless someone scrapes the paint.
features: Painted windows: a fingernail or a putty knife can scrape a clear patch in a minute
Coach's chair with its back to them
The parts-store box in the desk, if the party has not taken it
encounters: Coach, between 8 p.m. and midnight, packing a single suitcase
secrets: Scraping the paint off one window while Coach is in the room, at night, shows him to the lake. It is cruel, and it works. If the party does it, Old Glass will come for him (Act 2, Two Coaches).

keyLocations.name: The Dock and the Boathouse Slip
keyLocations.description: The swimming dock under the stars, every iron lantern post doubled in the still water; the Boathouse beside it, and under its floor the covered slip of black water where Old Glass goes down at dawn and comes up at dusk.
features: The end of the dock, where Gene knelt, where Curtis leaned out in 1962
The slip hatch in the Boathouse floor
Mist beginning on the water from three in the morning
encounters: The finale, if the party brings it here (Act 3, The Name)
secrets: The best place to say the name: Old Glass, called by its true name to its face, remembers, and walks back into the lake. Here it can walk straight down the dock into the water it came from. Anywhere else on the Neck it walks to the nearest shore and goes in.

keyLocations.name: The Outlet Bridge at Dawn
keyLocations.description: The bridge comes up out of the flood at about five in the morning, streaming, its rails hung with branches and weed, the road beyond it a mile of mud and gravel to the washout at Hemlock Run, which a Suburban in four-wheel drive can get through. The gatehouse with its cut line. The telephone pole. The Outlet still loud and fast and brown below.
features: The bridge deck: clear by 5 a.m., slick, passable at a crawl
The gatehouse porch, where Alvin waits from four in the morning with the ice pike and the mask
Running water under the deck: whatever is in a car that crosses it has been carried
encounters: The Suburban at 6:15, Coach driving, 'Santi' (or another borrowed face) in the passenger seat
secrets: Rule Four: if the thing has worn one living face from dusk to dawn unnamed, and the Suburban crosses the bridge with it before dusk on Monday, the trade is made. The moment the back wheels leave the deck, the real person, wherever they are, is gone, and their clothes are found folded on the Icehouse floor (or wherever they were) with lake water in the pockets. Old Glass in that face sits up in the passenger seat, warm for the first time in fifteen years, and starts to cry.
Alvin will try to stop the car with his body, the pike and a pile of stones across the deck he spent the small hours building. Coach will drive around it if he can and through it if he must.

synopsis: At dusk on Sunday, Santi Rivera, or whoever Coach has chosen, is missing. Coach took him to the Boathouse float with a lantern to 'check the boats' so the lake would see his face, and then locked him in the windowless Icehouse with Gene's body, 'safe from Alvin', where he cannot see the thing wearing his face and name himself to it. At nine 'Santi' knocks at the Lodge door; the party must find the real one, break into the Icehouse past Coach, and get Santi to look the thing in the eyes and say his name. If they do, Coach's plan is lost, and the thing, with no face left but the ones it saw tonight, wants the only face it ever really wanted: its own, which Coach is wearing. If it sees him, in a scraped window or on the dock, there are two Coaches on the Neck, and neither of them can say 'Curtis Seeley'. Through the small hours the water drops. Alvin waits at the bridge with his pike. At 6:15, if he can, Coach drives the Suburban down to the Outlet with a borrowed face in the passenger seat. The ending turns on a name: whether someone who knew Curtis Seeley will look the drowned man in the eyes and call him by it, on the dock or on the bridge, and whether Coach, at the last, will say his own.
hook: Sunday 18 September, 7:50 p.m. The sky is clear for the first time in two days, the lake is a sheet of black glass, and in the Lodge Opal is counting heads for the third time. "Santi," she says. "Where's Santi? He went down with Coach to look at the boats." Coach comes in at the back door, wiping his hands. "Santi's resting, pal. Cabin 7. He's had a hard day." Behind him, through the black window, out on the water, something is standing up to its waist off the end of the dock, looking at the Lodge.

conclusions.conclusion: Santi is in the Icehouse, and has to face the thing to take his face back
clues: E4: Coach's lie about Cabin 7, and Cabin 7 empty
The new padlock on the Icehouse door and Coach's key
Rule Four: the person must look it in the eyes and say their own name
'Santi' at the Lodge door at nine, unable to say Santi's name

conclusions.conclusion: Once it has lost the face Coach gave it, it will want its own
clues: F2: The Thin Place at the dock: it wants its own face
F4: if it sees Coach, it comes to the Director's House
Coach's terror of windows and the painted panes
Alvin: 'It's been looking for its face fifteen years. He knows it.'

conclusions.conclusion: Only its own name ends it, said to its face by someone who knew him
clues: C5: the 1888 log and Brodt; FOUND AND LAID
Rule Five, from any source in pc-scenario-003
Opal's shoebox of letters, to hold while she says it

acts.title: Sunday Night: Where Is Santi?
acts.description: From 7:50 to about eleven: the missing man, the second Santi, and the Icehouse. The purpose of this act is the rescue, and the first chance for the players to use the rules on purpose. If the party already has Coach in custody or has spoiled his plan, he has chosen someone else (the loneliest person on the Neck, often a player character who stood at a window) and locked them in the Icehouse the same way; adjust names, keep the shape.
objectives: Find out that Santi is not in Cabin 7
Meet 'Santi' at the door and know it for what it is
Find the real Santi in the Icehouse and get him out
Bring Santi face to face with the thing, and have him say his name

scenes.name: Cabin 7
scenes.description: Cabin 7 is dark. Gene's suitcase, Gene's wife's photograph, Santi's duffel. The beds are made. Santi is not there, and has not been since the morning. Wet bare prints come up the cinder path from the beach to the cabin's wooden sill and go in, and come out, and go back down to the lake. On the bed, a dent, cold and damp, where something sat. Coach, asked again, says he must have gone to the Playhouse, or the Dining Hall, he likes to be alone; Insight DC 12 catches the lie. Opal, if she is told, goes straight for Coach. Alvin, if he is with the party, says at once: "The Icehouse. No windows. That's where I'd put a man I didn't want seen." (CLUE E4.)
scenes.readAloud: Cabin 7 is dark and cold and smells of the lake. The beds are made. On the nightstand a woman in a photograph smiles at nobody. Santi's duffel is on the floor with his clothes folded on it, Army fashion. He is not here. On the end of the nearest bed there is a dent in the blanket, as if someone heavy had been sitting there for a long time, and when you put your hand on it, it is wet, and cold as the lake. On the floorboards, coming in from the screen door and going out again, bare footprints, filling slowly with water that is not there.

skillChecks.success: Two sets of tracks on the path. Bare wet feet, up from the lake and back. And Santi's boots and Coach's, this evening, going the other way: down to the Boathouse float, and then up the dam path, toward the Icehouse. Only Coach's come back.
skillChecks.failure: The cinder path is a mess of prints after two days of everyone walking it.

skillChecks.success: Coach is lying, and he is not good at it tonight; he has stopped trying to be. He knows you know. He is waiting to see if you will let him do it anyway.
skillChecks.failure: Coach says Santi wanted to be alone. People do, after a death.

scenes.name: Santi at the Door
scenes.description: At about nine, three knocks at the Lodge's front door, and Santi's voice: "Hey. It's me. Open up." It is Old Glass, wearing the face it was given at dusk, and it is wearing it well tonight: the jacket, the Bethlehem accent, the way Santi stands. It cannot say Santi's name; it cannot cross the iron sill unless Santi himself invites it. It wants to come in because Coach is somewhere it can smell, though it does not know why. Polaroid, hand mirror, a dark window: faceless. Rites (campaignRules): it can be put down with iron (back in the lake until tomorrow's dusk, which only helps Coach: the face it wore tonight is lost, so the trade fails, but Coach will choose again tomorrow and the water will be down) or, much better, Santi can be brought to it. It does not fight unless seized or cornered between iron and water. If the party leaves it, it walks the porch, looking in at every window, then goes along the shore toward the dam.
scenes.readAloud: Three knocks. The fire pops. "Hey," says Santi's voice through the door, easy, tired. "It's me. Open up, will you, it's freezing." Nobody moves. Opal's hand is over her mouth. Through the black window beside the door you can see him on the porch, under the porch light: Santi, in his jacket, hands in his pockets, stamping his feet a little against the cold, perfectly ordinary, perfectly himself, smiling at the window. And in the glass, laid over him like a second picture, the reflection of the same man is a grey shape standing on the porch boards with no face at all.

skillChecks.success: It is very good at Santi tonight, much better than it was at Gene. But it keeps looking past you into the room, at the corners, at the back door, at the stairs, like a dog that smells someone it knows in a house. It is not looking for Santi. It is looking for someone else.
skillChecks.failure: It is Santi. It is not Santi. It is standing on the porch asking to be let in.

skillChecks.success: It wore his face from dusk. If it wears it until dawn, unnamed, it only needs carrying. If Santi looks it in the eyes and says his own name before then, the face is his for good. Somewhere on the Neck, Santi has to be brought to this door. (Rule Four.)
skillChecks.failure: You know the rules. Knowing them on paper and standing a yard from it with the door open are different things.

scenes.name: The Icehouse
scenes.description: The Icehouse door has a new padlock. Coach has the key; he will not give it up, but he will not fight for it with anyone but Alvin. The party can break the lock (Mechanics DC 13, or a crowbar and Athletics DC 12, loud), go in by the roof hatch (Athletics DC 14), or talk Coach into opening it (Persuasion DC 15; DC 10 for Opal). Inside, in absolute darkness: the smell of sawdust, the shapes of canoes, and Santi's voice from beside the sawhorses, steady, "Who's that? Say your name." He has been here three hours with Gene. Dread 4. Fear check for the party entering, the sign of it, DC 10 (+2 dark), for the place itself. Then the hard part: Santi has to face the thing and say his name (Rule Four: fear check, the truth of it, DC 18 if he knows the rule; on a failure he cannot get the words out this round, and can try again). Bring them together, at the Lodge door, on the porch, on the path, and let the player (or the GM, for Santi) play it: two of the same young man, a yard apart, one warm and one wet, and one of them says, "I'm Santiago Rivera," and the other one runs out of its clothes onto the boards as lake water and weed. Everyone present: a fear check, the truth of it, DC 20, and then, because they did it on purpose, each loses 1 Dread for the courage of it.
scenes.readAloud: The lock gives. The door swings in on darkness so complete that your flashlight seems to make it worse: a cone of sawdust and stone and the curved hulls of canoes racked like the ribs of something, and the cold, the deep stone cold of a building made to keep ice through August. From the far end, by two sawhorses and a tarpaulin, a voice says, very steadily: "Who's that? Say your name." When you do, and your light finds him, Santi Rivera is sitting on the floor with his back against the sawhorse and his arms around his knees, and he has been crying, and he stands up anyway. "He's been by himself all day," he says, nodding at the tarp. "I didn't think he should be by himself." Then: "It's out there, isn't it. With my face."

skillChecks.success: Santi listens to the rule once, and nods, and says, 'Okay. Okay. I did worse in seventy-one.' He will go to it. He wants someone beside him. (Advantage on his fear check if a friend has a hand on his shoulder; a Chaplain's Steady Now first is better.)
skillChecks.failure: Santi is shaking too hard to stand up yet. Give him a minute. Give him the fire, a coffee, a hand on his arm. Then he will go.

skillChecks.success: The padlock is new and cheap. A screwdriver, a hairpin, the right twist, and it opens without a sound; Coach, if he is guarding the door, never hears it.
skillChecks.failure: The lock is cheap but your hands are cold and the light is bad. You can break the hasp instead, and the whole Neck will hear it.

encounters: Old Glass in Santi's face at the Lodge door (controlFile.oldGlass)
Coach at the Icehouse door from midnight, unarmed against anyone but Alvin; he steps aside for Opal

If the party puts Old Glass down with iron instead of bringing Santi to it, it goes back into the lake until dusk on Monday; Coach's plan fails tonight, the water goes down at five, and Coach tries to leave alone at dawn (Act 3)

acts.title: After Midnight: Two Coaches
acts.description: From about eleven to four. Santi's face is his own again, and Old Glass has lost the face Coach gave it. It still has the faces it has seen tonight at the lit windows, and it will take one if it must. But there is one face it wants more than all of them. If at any point tonight Coach is seen by the lake (at a window, on the porch, on the dock, through a scraped pane in the Director's House), Old Glass wears his face, and comes for him. The purpose of this act is the siege at its worst and Coach's choice. If the party keeps Coach hidden all night, Old Glass takes a face from a lit window instead (a player character's, if any stood at the glass), and the act becomes a hunt for a double before dawn; use the same scenes with that person in Coach's place.
objectives: Keep everyone alive through the small hours
Decide whether to show Coach to the lake
Face Coach with his own name

scenes.name: The Painted Window
scenes.description: The Director's House, or wherever Coach is. The party can do the cruellest thing in the campaign: scrape the paint off a lakeside window, or open the Lodge curtains with Coach in the room, or walk him onto the dock. Any of these lets the lake see him (Rule One), and from that moment Old Glass is wearing Coach's face, which is Curtis Seeley's face, which is its own. If the party does not do it, Alvin might (he has thought of it for fifteen years), or Coach himself might, at three in the morning, alone, scraping a hole in the paint with his thumbnail and looking out at the lake, because he is tired. Coach, if he is made to look, makes a sound nobody in the room will forget. Fear check for everyone, the truth of it, DC 20: in the black glass, behind Coach's reflection, a second figure, faceless, at his shoulder, and then not faceless.
scenes.readAloud: The paint comes off the glass in long cream curls under the knife, and behind it the night is very black and very still, and the lake beyond the porch lies like poured ink under the stars. Coach is in his chair with his back to it. He does not turn around. He does not have to. In the cleared pane you can see his reflection, the big shoulders, the grey head bowed, and behind his reflection, at its shoulder, as close as a man standing behind a barber's chair, another figure, grey, faceless, leaning in. Then its face fills in, all at once, like a photograph developing. It is his face. It is exactly his face. Coach closes his eyes and says, very quietly, in the old mountain voice, "There you are."

skillChecks.success: He is not surprised. He has seen that figure behind his reflection every night for fifteen years, in every dark window from here to Stroudsburg. What he is feeling is not fear, now. It is something like relief, and it is the worst thing you have seen this weekend.
skillChecks.failure: Coach sits with his eyes shut and his hands on his knees, and does not move.

skillChecks.success: Out on the lake, beyond the porch, something stands up out of the still water a hundred yards off the point and begins to wade ashore, slowly, the stars breaking around it.
skillChecks.failure: The lake is black and still. Nothing moves on it. Then, far out, a ring spreads.

scenes.name: Two Coaches
scenes.description: Old Glass, wearing Coach's face, comes ashore and walks to wherever Coach is: the Director's House, the Icehouse door, the Lodge. It is soaked, bareheaded, in a copy of the cardigan with the whistle on its lanyard. It cannot say his name, and neither can he. It does not attack him. It wants him to look at it. It will stand outside any iron sill and wait, and say, in his voice, the one thing it remembers clearly: "Opal?" At a wooden door it walks in. Two Coaches in one room: Insight DC 14 to tell which is which (the thing is wet, cold and does not fog the air). The mirror test fails here, and that is the horror of it: the real Coach has no face in a mirror or a photograph either (Rule Two, the taker's tell), so in the glass they are two grey shapes. Only a Polaroid separates them, barely: Coach develops as a blur, the thing as nothing at all. Alvin, if he is here, cannot tell either, and raises the pike over both. Coach can end it for himself in one breath, by looking it in the eyes and saying his own name, 'Lorenz Garside' (Rule Four): it loses his face forever and runs out of its clothes as lake water. Opal is in the room. Let the player who has been working on Coach all weekend ask him to. Let him decide.
scenes.readAloud: There are two of him. One is sitting in the chair with his hands on his knees, dry, grey-faced, old behind the eyes. The other is standing in the doorway, dripping, in the same cardigan and the same whistle on the same lanyard, his hair flat to his skull with lake water, a puddle spreading on the floor around his bare feet. The same big, kind, sunburned face. It looks at the man in the chair, and the man in the chair looks back, and neither of them says anything for a long time. Then the one in the doorway looks past him, round the room, at each of you, and finds Opal, and its face changes, opens, like a man who has heard a voice he knows across a crowd. "Opal?" it says. "Opal?"

skillChecks.success: Coach stands up. He walks to the thing in the doorway until they are a foot apart, and looks it in the eyes, and says, clearly, in the old voice, 'My name is Lorenz Garside. I was born in Larkin Corners in eighteen and eighty-six. I cut ice on this lake.' And the thing wearing his face looks at him with something like pity, and comes apart into lake water on the floor, and Coach sits down on the wet boards beside it and puts his face in his hands. Opal has heard every word. (Rule Four; Old Glass rises again at dusk, but never in this face.)
skillChecks.failure: Coach opens his mouth, and nothing comes. He tries. He cannot do it in front of her. 'I can't,' he says. 'I can't, I can't.' The thing in the doorway is still waiting for its sister to say something.

skillChecks.success: The thing in the doorway is not there for Coach. It came for its face, yes, but it is Opal it is looking at, and it has been trying to say something to her since it came in. A name. Hers, it can say. Its own, it cannot reach. Somebody has to give it to it. (Rule Five.)
skillChecks.failure: Two men with one face. One of them is a drowned thing. You are not sure, in this light, which.

scenes.name: The Light Goes Out
scenes.description: This scenario's one 'light goes out at the worst moment': at about 2 a.m., wherever the party is and whatever is happening, the Icehouse generator runs out of gas (Victor or anyone with Mechanics knows there is a can in the Boathouse workshop, a hundred yards along the shore in the dark). Every electric light on the Neck goes out. The Lodge has its fire; the Director's House has nothing; flashlights have about four hours of batteries (dread.json light_and_dark), and the party have been using them since Saturday. In the dark, under the stars, the lake is a black mirror that reflects nothing but stars, and every one of the faces Old Glass has seen tonight could be the one coming along the shore path. Whoever goes for the gas meets, in the dark on the shore, someone they know, who says, 'It's me. Don't be scared.' The player should not be told whether it is.
scenes.readAloud: The lights go out. Not one at a time: all of them, every bulb on the Neck at once, and the generator's far-off stutter stops in the middle of a cough, and there is nothing but starlight on still water and the spillway's roar. Somewhere along the shore path, between you and the Boathouse, a flashlight is coming toward you, bobbing, and a voice behind it you know as well as your own says, softly, "It's me. Don't be scared. It's only me."

skillChecks.success: The flashlight is real, and the hand holding it is warm, and the breath that comes with the voice fogs in the cold air, which the thing's breath never does. It is them. Probably. Ask their name. (Rule Two.)
skillChecks.failure: A friend with a flashlight, in the dark, saying your name. Say theirs. Wait for them to say it back.

skillChecks.success: Gas in, choke out, three pulls, and the Onan catches; the Lodge windows go yellow across the water, doubled in the lake. You have two hours before it needs more.
skillChecks.failure: The cord, the choke, the cord. It floods. Five minutes in the dark, with the Icehouse door open behind you and the stars on the water.

encounters: Old Glass in Coach's face, or another borrowed face if Coach was never seen; it fights only if seized or blocked from its own face or the water
Alvin Dreher (Masked Killer), if he has not been talked down: he goes to wherever two of anybody are, with the pike and the mirror
Coach (Night Watchman) with the office revolver: he will shoot Alvin to protect himself, and he will not shoot the thing with his face

acts.title: Monday Dawn: The Name
acts.description: From about four to sunrise at 6:45. The water goes off the bridge at five. If the thing is wearing a face it has worn since dusk, unnamed, it has only to be carried over the Outlet before Monday dusk, and Coach has his spare rotor, unless the party has taken it. Alvin is at the gatehouse. The ending is whichever of controlFile.outcomes the players make, and the scene that decides it is a name said aloud. Give the players every chance to get Opal (or Winnie, Nell or Odessa) face to face with Old Glass, in whatever face, with a light to see by.
objectives: Get the one who knew him face to face with Old Glass
Call it Curtis Seeley, to its face
Stop the Suburban, or the man in the mask, or both, at the bridge
See the sun come up on Lantern Lake

scenes.name: The Bridge
scenes.description: At five the bridge comes up out of the flood, streaming. At four Alvin went down to the gatehouse in the mask with the pike and built a wall of stones across the deck. At 6:15, if Coach's plan is still alive (the thing is wearing a face it has worn since dusk, unnamed) or if Coach is simply running, the Suburban comes down from the lot with its lights on, Coach at the wheel, and beside him, sitting very upright, whoever the thing is wearing. Alvin walks out into the headlights with the pike. The party can be anywhere. Coach will drive around the stones if he can (Driving DC 13 for him) and through Alvin if he must, and he does not want to. Alvin will put the pike through the windshield. If the car crosses with the thing in it unnamed, the trade is made (Rule Four). If it crosses with only Coach, nothing happens but that Coach is gone, and the thing is still in the lake, and the masks are in the box. Let the players decide what they stop.
scenes.readAloud: The flood has gone down in the night like a breath let out, and the bridge stands up out of the brown water, streaming, its rails hung with branches and weed. Across the deck, in the grey before sunrise, somebody has built a low wall of stones from the stream bed, and on the gatehouse porch beside it a big man in a wool mackinaw and a pale carved mask is sitting with an ice pike across his knees, waiting. Up the road, at the top of the lot, headlights come on. An engine turns over, catches, and runs. The camp Suburban comes down the hill toward the bridge, slowly, and in its passenger seat, lit green by the dashboard, someone is sitting very upright with their hands folded in their lap.

skillChecks.success: You get to the road in front of the Suburban before it reaches the stones, and stand there in its headlights with your hand up, and it stops. Coach looks at you through the windshield for a long time. Then he turns off the engine and puts his forehead on the wheel.
skillChecks.failure: You are too far. The Suburban reaches the stones, swings to go round them, and the masked man stands up off the gatehouse porch and walks out into its lights with the pike raised. Somebody has to choose, now, which of them to stop.

skillChecks.success: Alvin is going to die on that bridge rather than let the car cross, and Coach is going to drive it across rather than stay. Neither of them wants to kill the other. Both of them will.
skillChecks.failure: A car, a masked man, a bridge, the dawn coming. Move.

scenes.name: The Name
scenes.description: Wherever the party brings them together, on the dock, the bridge, the Lodge porch, the Suburban's open door: someone who knew Curtis Seeley in life, Opal by preference, Winnie, Nell or Odessa, or anyone holding Opal's shoebox of his letters and telling his story, looks Old Glass in the eyes, in whatever face it is wearing, and says, 'Curtis Seeley.' (Rites That Work: an Occult check DC 15 to say it so that it hears, with advantage for those who knew him; Opal's player or the GM rolls; a Chaplain's Graveside gives advantage too; a failure means the words came out wrong, too fast, too frightened, and they can try again next round.) It remembers. Its borrowed face becomes, for one breath, Curtis's own, broad and sunburned and thirty, the face from the 1962 photograph, and it says 'Opal?', and she says yes. Then it turns and walks back to the water (down the dock, if they are on the dock; down the bank to the Outlet pool, if they are at the bridge, and it walks into running water as if it were nothing) and goes down into the lake, and lies down, and the lake is only water. Every character present drops to Dread 0 (dread.json recovery). If Coach is there, he can say the name 'Curtis Seeley' for the first time in fifteen years, and he does, and his face comes back into the Suburban's mirror, old.
scenes.readAloud: Opal walks out to it with the shoebox held against her chest like a hymnal. The thing stands in the grey light, dripping, in someone else's face, and watches her come, and does not move. She stops a yard from it and looks it in the eyes. "Curtis," she says. Her voice cracks and she makes it stop. "Curtis Seeley. You are Curtis Seeley. You swam this lake end to end every Labor Day. You wrote me from Korea every week. You're my brother." And the face on it changes. Not all at once. Like a reflection when the water stills: the borrowed features slide, settle, and it is a broad, sunburned, laughing face of thirty, the face from the 1962 photograph, wet, astonished. "Opal?" it says. "Yes," she says. "Yes." Then it turns away from her, gently, and walks back down to the water, and into it, and the lake closes over it without a ring, and the first light comes over the hills and lies on Lantern Lake, and it is only water.

skillChecks.success: It hears. It remembers. (Rule Five; the outcome is THE NAME, controlFile.outcomes.)
skillChecks.failure: The name comes out wrong, too fast, half-swallowed, and the thing only tilts its head. It is still listening. Try again: slower, to its face, as if to a man you love who is going deaf.

skillChecks.success: Coach, watching, is weeping. When it has gone he says, aloud, as if trying a word in a foreign language, 'Curtis.' And again. 'Curtis Seeley.' And then he looks at his reflection in the Suburban's window, and for the first time in fifteen years it has a face, and it is an old man's.
skillChecks.failure: The lake is still. The sun is coming up. Everyone is very quiet.

scenes.name: Sunrise on Lantern Lake
scenes.description: The epilogue. Whatever the ending, give it its cost (controlFile.outcomes). At about noon the State Police come over the bridge in two cars, with a Ridgeview executive behind them in a Cadillac, to a dead surveyor in the Icehouse, a caretaker who says at once, 'I killed him. I thought he was something else,' and a party of very tired people. Alvin goes with them and does not resist. What Coach does depends on the ending: in THE NAME, he asks Nolan to take his statement, all of it, and begins it 'My name is Lorenz Garside', and nobody in Stroudsburg will believe a word, and Opal sits beside him while he says it; in THE RETURN, a forty-five-year-old man who does not know what year it is sits shaking in the Lodge wrapped in a blanket calling his sister's name, and nobody can find Coach; in COACH'S BARGAIN, someone the players love is in the lake, and they know its name now, and the masks are in the box, and next September is a long way off. The sale closes at ten, or does not; Ridgeview will build its three hundred houses, or will hear that the lake is haunted and quietly sell the Neck to the state. Winnie goes to her sister's in Hazleton on Tuesday. Marvin plays the Lantern Lake Waltz once more on the Lodge piano before they lock up. Let the players talk.
scenes.readAloud: The sun comes up over the eastern hills and lies flat and gold across Lantern Lake from shore to shore. Mist lifts off the water in slow sheets. A heron stands in the shallows by the dock, motionless, and then flies. The lake is very clear this morning. You can see down into it a long way, the old log booms of the cutting channels lying on the bottom like the ribs of a ship, and your own face on the surface looking back at you, and it moves when you move, exactly when you move, and is only a reflection. Up at the Lodge, through the open door, someone is playing a slow waltz on the piano.

skillChecks.success: Nolan's report, or Paula's story, gets told the way the players want it told. The State Police take down every word and believe the parts about the ice pike. Paula's editor runs the feature, and a single Polaroid of a dock at night with a smudge on it, captioned LANTERN NIGHT, 1977.
skillChecks.failure: Nobody in Stroudsburg wants to hear about Old Glass. The report says a caretaker killed a surveyor during a storm, and the rest is grief.

skillChecks.success: Opal, on the dock with the shoebox, is not crying. She is looking at the lake as if she were reading it, and when you sit down beside her she says, "He said my name." That is all.
skillChecks.failure: Everyone is too tired to speak, and that is all right.

encounters: Alvin Dreher at the bridge (Masked Killer): he will fight the Suburban and anyone who tries to move him, and will stop at once for Winnie, Opal, or the name said aloud on the dock
Coach (Night Watchman) at the wheel: he will not fire on anyone but Alvin
Old Glass in its last face: it does not fight now; it is waiting for someone to say a word

npcsInvolved.name: 'Coach' Seeley, 45 (Lorenz Garside, born 1886)
npcsInvolved.role: Director; the man who raised it, and the one who can still end his part of it
npcsInvolved.description: Packing one suitcase; guarding the Icehouse with the office revolver; in his chair with his back to a painted window; at the wheel of the Suburban at dawn.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To leave before Monday dusk with the thing gone into someone else's life. Under that, to never say his own name in front of Opal. Under that, to be forgiven.

npcsInvolved.name: Old Glass, which is Curtis Seeley
npcsInvolved.description: In Santi's face at dusk; in Coach's face if it sees him; at the end, for one breath, its own.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Its face, its name, its sister. Mostly, now, its name.

npcsInvolved.name: Opal Seeley, 41
npcsInvolved.role: Sister (a companion); the one who can say the name
npcsInvolved.description: The shoebox of letters held against her chest.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To bring her brother home, or to let him rest.

npcsInvolved.name: Santiago "Santi" Rivera, 25
npcsInvolved.description: Three hours in the dark with Gene; then the bravest thing anyone does all weekend.
npcsInvolved.motivation: His name. His face. To get Gene home.

npcsInvolved.name: Alvin Dreher, 58
npcsInvolved.role: The man in the mask, at the bridge
npcsInvolved.description: Philomena's mask, the pike, a wall of stones across the deck.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Nothing crosses. And then, if the name is said, to take the mask off by the water for the first time in his life.

npcsInvolved.name: Winifred "Winnie" Szot, 63
npcsInvolved.description: Philomena's letter in her purse; coffee at four in the morning; the voice Alvin stops for.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To see everyone through to morning.

npcsInvolved.name: Roscoe Talmadge, 50
npcsInvolved.description: Reads the river for the hour the bridge comes clear; tracks the wet prints in the dark.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Get them all over that bridge in daylight, the right way.

npcsInvolved.name: Marvin Eckhart, 64
npcsInvolved.description: The 1958 Lantern Lake Waltz, with the doors open.

rewards.money: There is no payment for this. Ridgeview Leisure Communities pays Gene Marcotte's widow his life insurance and sends the party a letter asking them not to speak to the press. Coach's offer of the purchase money to Opal stands in THE NAME, if he lives to sign it; she gives half of it to Gene's widow. Paula's feature earns her $150 and a byline on the front of the Sunday section. The State Police pay nobody for anything.
items: Philomena Delamater's 1934 mask, which Alvin gives to whoever said the name, if it was said
Opal's shoebox of letters, and Curtis Seeley's whistle on its lanyard if THE NAME was the ending (it is found on the dock in the morning, wet)
Lorenz Garside's pocket watch, L.G. 1907, given to Nolan with Coach's statement
The Lantern Lake Ice Company night log, which Zachary is allowed to take for the Pennsylvania state archives

twists: The rescue is the trap. Saving Santi breaks Coach's plan and frees Old Glass to want the only face it ever wanted. The better the party does on Sunday night, the more likely it is that there are two Coaches by three in the morning.
Coach can save himself at any moment by saying "Lorenz Garside" to its face. He has known that all weekend. Whether he does it, in front of Opal, is his ending, and the players can only ask.

The name works in any face. Opal does not have to wait for it to wear Coach's, or Curtis's. She can say it to a thing wearing Santi, or Gene, or a player character, and it will remember. The players may not realise that until someone tries.

Alvin's wall of stones across the bridge is the right idea for the wrong reason. If the thing is named before dawn, there is nothing in the car to stop; if it is not, he is the last thing between the lake and the world, and he is fifty-eight and has not slept since Thursday.
In THE NAME, Old Glass walks into the Outlet pool if that is the nearest water, running water and all, because it is no longer bound by anything. Nobody should try to stop it.
dmTips: Check in before this session. It has a person shut in the dark with a body, a man forced to see his own face, and a drowned man walking back into a lake. Honour 'skip that' at once by cutting to dawn. Old Glass walking into the lake at the end is a man going home to rest, never a death and never a despair; describe it so.
Run the night as a siege on a clock: tell the players the hour at every scene change, and say when the bridge will be clear. They should feel dawn coming as something they want and dread at once.

The best ending needs Opal (or Winnie, Nell or Odessa) face to face with the thing with a light. If the players have kept her safe in the Lodge all night, that is right and good; now they have to bring her out. Let them plan it.

Coach's choice in Two Coaches is the campaign's emotional peak. Give it room. The player who has been working on him should get to ask. The GM decides, honestly, whether a man who spent forty-eight years in the dark can say his own name in front of the woman whose brother he became. A roll helps; it does not decide.

The bridge is a set piece with three parties and a car. Keep it short and physical: headlights, stones, a pike through a windshield, a choice. Nobody needs to die on it, and Alvin should not, unless the players let him.

If the players fail, and the trade is made, say so plainly and gently in the epilogue, and give them the rules and the name to carry: the thing that drove away in their friend's face is Curtis Seeley, and their friend is in the lake, and next September someone could say their name on the dock.
Budget an hour and a half for Sunday night and the Icehouse, an hour for the small hours, and an hour for the bridge, the name and the epilogue.
